In adults with hypertension requiring pharmacological treatment, the choice of combination therapy (e.g., beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, diuretics, ACE inhibitors, or ARBs) as first-line agents was evaluated based on systematic review evidence. 23. Subgroup analysis by ethnicity showed consistent evidence in both Asian and non-Asian populations. 24. A range of individual and social factors, such as lack of familial support, need for separate meals, sense of security, local amenities, and availability of healthy food, were identified as challenges to treatment adherence. 30. Perceptions of symptoms, disease management, and treatment expectations also influence adherence. Quality of life on antihypertensive therapy is a critical issue, as clinicians often prescribe medications to asymptomatic patients who may experience adverse effects. 31. Amlodipine, a calcium channel blocker, is one of the most commonly prescribed medications for hypertension. Despite its availability as a generic, the cost remains significant, especially for patients with multiple comorbidities requiring additional medications. 32. Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ), a thiazide diuretic, is a cost-effective first-line option for hypertension treatment. When administered separately, HCTZ and captopril are effective and economical alternatives to more expensive medications like amlodipine. 33. High drug costs, often paid out-of-pocket by patients, can reduce medication adherence and indirectly impact national economies. In China, studies have shown that out-of-pocket costs for antihypertensive medications reduce adherence among patients with hypertension and cardiovascular disease.
